title: When Your Leader Tells You to Part Ways With One of Your Direct Reports
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership field note tackles an awkward middle-management dilemma: a senior leader forms a negative view of one of your team members, often from limited direct exposure, and strongly suggests you let that person go, while you see more value in their work. The piece notes that arguing the team member is better than the leader thinks rarely changes the senior leader's mind and usually ends with 'it's your call' plus lingering advice to act, which puts your own reputation at stake. It rejects the passive strategy of hoping the team member redeems themselves and instead lays out a plan built on candor in both directions: a specific timeline and observable improvement markers shared upward, and a concrete, honest conversation with the team member about what triggered the scrutiny. Regular, honest updates keep the senior leader from assuming you lack the will to act. The closing argument is that credibility is judged not by whether you agreed with the recommendation but by whether you acted on evidence rather than instinct or avoidance.
points: Senior leaders rarely mandate a termination, but a strong signal that you have a weak link creates a reputational dilemma if you keep the person without a plan.

Defending the team member's hidden value or institutional knowledge seldom changes a senior leader's mind; a specific timeline with observable markers of improvement does more to show you took the concern seriously.
Protecting a team member without telling them they need protecting only delays the inevitable, so they must hear concretely what triggered scrutiny and what closing the gap requires.
Going silent after presenting a plan signals a lack of will, so regular and honest progress updates are part of preserving trust from above.
When a retained team member eventually proves the senior leader right and the manager never acted, the manager's objectivity and judgment become suspect.
quotes: Making the case that this team member is better than the leader believes, or that they have institutional knowledge or relationships that make them hard to replace, will rarely change the leader’s mind. At best, it usually results in the leader declaring it is your call, but that they still advise you to make a change at some point soon.

The wrong strategy is to ignore this advice and hope the team member can redeem themselves at some point. If you’re going to hang on to this team member despite your leader’s recommendation, you need a plan.
The plan starts with candor in both directions. Go back to your leader with a specific timeline and the observable markers of improvement you will be tracking. Vague reassurances don’t cut it.

They need to know in concrete terms exactly what performance or behavior triggered this scrutiny and what closing the gap requires. Protecting the team member without telling them they need protecting only delays the inevitable and almost always ends poorly.

Prove that isn’t the case by giving your leader regular updates. Be honest about whether progress is being made. If the team member has grown and you have real evidence of improvement, make the case with your leader.

The leader who acts on evidence, rather than on instinct or avoidance, is the one who earns lasting trust from above. Your credibility as a leader is judged not by whether you agreed with the recommendation, but by how honestly and objectively you handled it.
